question: Give an example of making a decision that prioritized the customer/client even when it conflicted with short-term internal metrics or convenience.

raiseTranscript.text: Give an example of making a decision that prioritized the customer even when it conflicted with short-term internal metrics or convenience.

I was on support handling tickets. SLA was 4 hours to first response. A customer had a billing issue that needed me to dig into their account history. It took 90 minutes instead of the usual 15. I stayed with it instead of escalating or closing it out.
What happened with your metrics that day?
I missed my target for tickets closed. My manager flagged it in the 1:1 but I explained the customer got their refund same day and left a positive note. She said it was the right call.

raiseNotes: Q: Give an example of making a decision that prioritized the customer even when it conflicted with short-term internal metrics or convenience.
Role: L2 support agent, 9 months tenure
Situation: Billing ticket required deep account work vs quick close
Action: Spent 90 min instead of 15 min SLA target
Outcome: Customer resolved same day, positive note; manager noted it in 1:1
Quote: "I explained the customer got their refund same day and left a positive note."
Follow-up: Asked about metrics impact - candidate owned the miss but tied it to customer result
junior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for junior. The candidate described choosing extra time on one ticket over hitting daily close count. Quote shows they explained the outcome to their manager rather than hiding the metric miss. Story stays within individual scope and shows basic ownership of the trade-off. The follow-up confirms they understood the metric was secondary. Biggest strength is linking the longer effort directly to same-day resolution instead of generic "customer first" language.

lowerTranscript.text: Give an example of making a decision that prioritized the customer even when it conflicted with short-term internal metrics or convenience.
There was a customer who wanted a feature we didn't have. I told them we'd look into it but didn't push internally because my ticket volume was already behind.

lowerNotes: Q: Give an example of making a decision that prioritized the customer even when it conflicted with short-term internal metrics or convenience.
Candidate defaulted to internal ticket volume as reason not to advocate
No concrete action taken for the customer beyond a standard reply
Follow-up: Asked for outcome - candidate said the ticket was closed without escalation
junior.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar for junior. The example shows the candidate prioritizing their own ticket count over any customer action. No evidence of even attempting to escalate or document the request. The story ends with the ticket closed, offering no learning or ownership. Gap is absence of any decision that actually favored the customer.

raiseTranscript.text: Give an example of making a decision that prioritized the customer even when it conflicted with short-term internal metrics or convenience.

We were launching a new reporting dashboard. The PM wanted to ship with last month's data only to hit the quarterly OKR. I pushed to delay by two weeks so we could include real-time filters after hearing from three enterprise customers that stale data would break their workflow.
How did that land with the PM and metrics?

The launch slipped and we missed the OKR by 8%. Two of those customers renewed at higher tiers three months later citing the real-time feature. I documented the feedback loop for the next planning cycle.

raiseNotes: Q: Give an example of making a decision that prioritized the customer even when it conflicted with short-term internal metrics or convenience.
Role: Senior engineer on platform team
Situation: Dashboard launch vs real-time filter request from enterprise accounts
Action: Advocated for two-week delay despite quarterly OKR
Outcome: Missed OKR by 8% but two renewals attributed to the feature
Quote: "Two of those customers renewed at higher tiers three months later citing the real-time feature."
Follow-up: Confirmed cross-functional pushback and how it was handled
senior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for senior. The candidate influenced a launch decision across PM and engineering to protect enterprise workflow. They accepted the OKR miss and later connected it to measurable renewal impact. Story shows cross-team influence without authority and use of customer quotes to justify the trade-off. Biggest strength is closing the loop by feeding the outcome back into planning rather than stopping at the delay itself.

I once asked the PM to add a filter but they said no because of the deadline so we shipped without it.

lowerNotes: Q: Give an example of making a decision that prioritized the customer even when it conflicted with short-term internal metrics or convenience.

No follow-up action or customer impact measured
Follow-up: No evidence of attempting to quantify the customer risk
senior.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar for senior. The candidate raised the issue once and stopped when told no. No attempt to gather or present customer evidence that could have changed the decision. Story lacks any measurable outcome or influence attempt beyond the initial ask.

raiseTranscript.text: Give an example of making a decision that prioritized the customer even when it conflicted with short-term internal metrics or convenience.

My team was measured on support ticket volume. One enterprise customer had repeated onboarding friction. I pulled two engineers off rotation for a week to build a guided setup flow even though it dropped our team's monthly ticket count by 12%.
How did you handle the metric review with your director?
I showed the drop in repeat tickets from that account and the renewal that followed. We changed the team goal to include repeat-issue rate the next quarter.

raiseNotes: Q: Give an example of making a decision that prioritized the customer even when it conflicted with short-term internal metrics or convenience.
Role: Support manager, 5 reports
Situation: Ticket volume goal vs enterprise onboarding pain
Action: Redirected two engineers for a week to build self-serve flow
Outcome: 12% ticket drop offset by lower repeat issues and renewal
Quote: "We changed the team goal to include repeat-issue rate the next quarter."
Follow-up: Asked how the metric change was socialized upward
manager.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for manager. The candidate traded team productivity metrics for a targeted customer fix and then used the result to adjust the team's goals. Story shows they protected the team from short-term volume pressure while creating longer-term leverage. Biggest strength is translating the customer win into a permanent metric change rather than a one-off exception.

Follow-up: Candidate could not name a specific customer outcome
manager.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar for manager. The candidate gave a generic directive without reallocating resources or changing how success was measured. Story shows no actual trade-off was made or defended upward.

raiseTranscript.text: Give an example of making a decision that prioritized the customer even when it conflicted with short-term internal metrics or convenience.

We had a product line that was 18% of revenue but 40% of support cost. The CFO wanted to raise prices to improve margin. I chose to sunset the line over 18 months and migrate customers to a higher-tier offering with better margins and lower support load.
What was the revenue impact in year one?

We took a 7% revenue hit in that segment but support costs dropped 22% company-wide and net retention in the migrated base rose 9 points. We used the freed capacity to launch two new enterprise features.

raiseNotes: Q: Give an example of making a decision that prioritized the customer even when it conflicted with short-term internal metrics or convenience.
Role: VP Product, P&L owner for a business unit
Situation: High-support low-margin product line vs short-term revenue target
Action: Chose sunsetting and migration instead of price increase
Outcome: 7% revenue dip offset by 22% support reduction and +9pt retention
Quote: "We used the freed capacity to launch two new enterprise features."
Follow-up: Confirmed the multi-quarter trade-off and how it was communicated to board
exec.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for exec. The candidate made a portfolio-level decision to exit a product rather than extract short-term margin from customers. They accepted a measurable revenue dip in exchange for structural cost and retention gains. Story demonstrates long-term judgment and use of the decision to create capacity for new work. Biggest strength is framing the choice around customer migration success rather than internal cost avoidance.

lowerTranscript.text: Give an example of making a decision that prioritized the customer even when it conflicted with short-term internal metrics or convenience.
We raised prices on the low-margin product and offered credits to the biggest complainers.

lowerNotes: Q: Give an example of making a decision that prioritized the customer even when it conflicted with short-term internal metrics or convenience.
Decision stayed inside existing product and metrics
No structural change or customer migration path
Follow-up: No long-term customer or P&L outcome provided
exec.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar for exec. The candidate chose a tactical price adjustment that protected short-term numbers without addressing the underlying customer friction. Story shows no strategic trade-off or multi-quarter thinking.
